question: What's the most important to prevent AVN in talus Fx
options:
A) Reduction to <2 mm
B) Minimizing the sinus tarsi and tarsal canal dissection decreases risk of AVN
C) Fixation<24hr 
D) Medial mal osteotomy
consensus_answer: B. Minimizing the sinus tarsi dissection decreases risk of AVN
evidence:
This is a repeat from Res study - answer is B
Medial mal osteotomy? An osteotomy of the medial malleolus exposes the medial aspect of the body of the talus and allows the surgeon to protect the posteromedial deltoid branches from the posterior tibial artery which is the main blood supply to the body of the talus. (AO Surg Ref); Blackbook p.103 - should not dissect deltoid ligament, inferior talus neck and sinus tarsi to preserve blood supply to the talus (Foot Ankle Surg 2018)
agree with B
+1 for med mal osteotomy.
- Not medial mal osteotomy, bet on my right hand its B. Most recent big talus paper from Vallier 2024 emphasizes that more dissection leads to AVN. The talus tarsal canal is the most dominant blood supply to the talus and would not want to dissect there

66.A patient with an osteoid osteoma of the C5 lamina is seen in clinic. She has been refractory to non-op treatment. 
What is the next step?
a)Radiofrequency ablation 
b)En bloc resection 
Curettage and bone grafting
evidence:
JAAOS 2012 (Benign Tumors of the Spine): Management begins with AINS. If this is unsuccessful, then minimally invasive techniques such as RFA effectively destroy the lesion. However, proximity of the lesion to neural structures may preclude the use of RFA (risk of thermal damage to adjacent neural structures). En bloc excision is recommended in patients with OO with associated fixed spinal deformity, with neurologic compression or if RFA is deemed unsafe due to the anatomic location or has been previously unsuccessful.

BJR 2020: Spinal osteoid osteomas account for 10% cases of all cases with posterior elements being the most common location. While ablating spinal osteoid osteomas, extreme care must be taken to avoid injury to neural elements, vessels and facet joint. A shelf of bone should always be present between the spinal cord and the tip of the probe.

Eur Spine J 2007: although with the limitations of a small casuistry and rarity of the pathology, indicates that PRC in the treatment of cervical osteoid osteoma is equally effective to surgery with respect to the control of symptoms. Frequent localization in the posterior arch presents the problem of secondary instability with surgical excision. Extensive and unbalanced approaches require associated posterior fusion. PRC can replace extensive surgical approaches for OO of the posterior arch and of the joint pillar, obtaining remission of the symptoms with a mini-invasive technique that has demonstrated to be applicable also in vicinity of noble and fragile structures such as the vertebral artery, spinal cord and nerve roots. The highlights of this technique include: local anesthesia, direct control of the neurological functions, meticulous execution of the technique, i.e., cauterization positioning, dispersed cauterization, duration of the application, and cauterization temperatures.

question:
86F undergoing THA for OA. What is true regarding THA fixation?
a.Hybrid (uncemented cup and cemented stem) has best track record in registry for this population
b.Same 1-year revision rate regardless of fixation method
c.When using cemented stems, no difference in implant longevity between polished taper and composite beam designs
d.Aim for 2-3 mm of cement mantle on both acetabular and femoral sides
evidence:
The following steps must be taken to ensure appropriate cementation on the acetabular side. Reaming must perforate the sclerotic bone down to bleeding cancellous bone. Additional drill holes are created circumferentially to allow cement penetration. Bone graft can be placed on the medial/inferior wall to help increase cement pressurization and sealing the acetabulum.32 The bone surface must then be dried. One bag of cement is then prepared using vacuum mixing to reduce porosity. Once the ideal viscosity is reached, the cement is inserted into the acetabulum and pressurized over the entire cement mantle. One must plan for an even 2- to 3-mm cement mantle around the component. The all polyethylene cemented acetabular implant must then be inserted in the ideal orientation and completely buried within the boundary of the bony acetabulum.33 Constant pressure must be applied until the cement hardens.

Similar principles must be respected on the femoral side. The ideal size centralizers and cement restrictor are measured. A cement restrictor is placed at the ideal depth and the centralizer affected at the tip of the stem. The centralizer will allow for 2- to 3-mm cement mantle uniformly around the stem.

B. Other compartment OA 
C. Infection 
D. poly dislocation
evidence:
Should this not be D?? Unicompartmental Knee Arthroplasty: Modes of Failure and Conversion to Total Knee Arthroplasty (2017)
The main causes of UKA failure include bearing dislocation (in mobile designs), aseptic mechanical loosening, polyethylene wear, progression of osteoarthritis (OA) in unreplaced compartments, infection, impingement, periprosthetic fracture, retaining of cement debris into the joint, arthrofibrosis, and unexplained pain. Bearing dislocation continues to be advocated as the predominant mechanism of failure in mobile UKA, whereas polyethylene wear and aseptic loosening remains the main cause of failure of fixed UKA. Degeneration of the unreplaced compartments has been reported in both mobile and fixed designs. Regardless of the implant design, most of the failures occur in medial UKA when compared with lateral

Radial head overstuffing puts stain on LUCL leading to instablity in supination. Many papers saying overstuffing leads to instablity. They are asking spesifcially in supination where mcl is protected and wouldent casue instbality.  How does everyone feel about switching over to C as the answer?Here is one example from Dr.King at western: ARTHROPLASTY OVERSTUFFING,JBJS 2010. overstuffing the radial head can lead to pain, decreased range of motion, capitellar wear, and instability in the elbow joint. Ipsilateral femoral neck and shaft fractures occur in 2.5% to 6% of femur fractures. The injury results from high energy trauma. Victims are usually young, with multiple associated injuries. The diagnosis of the neck fracture is delayed in 19% to 31% of patients. The neck fracture line is almost vertical and nondisplaced, or minimally displaced in 26% to 59% of cases. The shaft fracture is often midshaft and open, and/or comminuted in 47% to 67% of cases. b.        Pemberton
c.        Salter

evidence:
Selberg, Courtney M. MD; Chidsey, Berrien MSMI, CMI; Skelton, Anne BS; Mayer, Stephanie MD. Pelvic Osteotomies in the Child and Young Adult Hip: Indications and Surgical Technique. Journal of the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons 28(6):p e230-e237, March 15, 2020. | DOI: 10.5435/JAAOS-D-19-00223
In children and young adults, pelvic osteotomies are used for hip preservation including femoral head coverage improvement and hip joint stabilization. There are three main categories used by hip preservation surgeons as follows:
Redirectional: These are incomplete osteotomies which aim to reduce the overall volume and redirect the acetabulum by a hinge located at the triradiate cartilage and/or pubic symphysis. These include Salter, Pemberton, Dega, and San Diego osteotomies.
Reorientation: These are complete osteotomies which aim to reorient the entire acetabulum including periacetabular and triple osteotomies.
Salvage: These are osteotomies which aim to enlarge the acetabulum and/or improve femoral head coverage by medializing the hip center, most often in an incongruent or arthritic hip joint that is not an appropriate candidate for a reorientation osteotomy. These include shelf and Chiari osteotomies.
Shelf osteotomies were the main surgical treatment for acetabular dysplasia until reorientation osteotomies became more popular and proved more effective.35 Staheli's shelf osteotomy creates an acetabular shelf to restore femoral head coverage and increase hip stability through the creation of a slot in the ilium for a bone graft.36 This osteotomy is a salvage procedure as bone is used to increase coverage versus articular cartilage
Chiari Osteotomy: in 1974, which uses medial displacement of the cancellous bone of the ilium to better distribute the load of the hip joint.
